pages.searchText: Authentication Decision Model Relevant source files MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md README.md Purpose and Scope The Authentication Decision Model in SecureKit governs how multi-modal biometric signals (keystroke dynamics, face verification, voice recognition, and ID card OCR/matching) are combined with contextual risk indicators (IP geolocation, VPN/proxy/Tor detection) to evaluate user authenticity README.md 9-14 This page details the ingestion of signals, challenge-response lifecycles, consent recording, session tracking, and the risk evaluation logic that yields one of three terminal outcomes: allow, step_up, or deny README.md 14 1. Multi-Modal Signal Ingestion SecureKit evaluates a heterogeneous set of biometric and contextual vectors to verify identity without relying strictly on static secrets: Keystroke Dynamics: Captures precise keydown and keyup telemetry (dwell time and flight latency) via the web SDK. It evaluates both dynamic typing cadence against Exponential Moving Average (EMA) profiles and static challenge text verification README.md 9 MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 125-126 Face Verification: Processes frame captures through MTCNN and FaceNet pipelines to extract facial embeddings, perform liveness checks, and manage reference profiles via a sliding window mechanism README.md 10 Voice Verification: Ingests audio samples validated against random challenge phrases via Whisper for transcription accuracy and SpeechBrain for speaker similarity matching README.md 11 Card Verification: Combines document capture, PaddleOCR text extraction, and OpenCLIP visual similarity scoring to authenticate government-issued identification cards README.md 12 Network & IP Context: Queries IP intelligence services (such as VPNAPI) to flag VPNs, proxies, Tor exit nodes, data center traffic, and geolocation anomalies against defined country access policies README.md 13 Sources: README.md 7-14 MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 125-126 2. Challenge, Consent, and Session Management SecureKit enforces cryptographic and stateful controls surrounding user interactions through dedicated storage managers and endpoints: Challenge Generation and Consumption: Handled via POST /challenge/text and POST /challenge/text/consume. Challenges maintain a strict default Time-To-Live (TTL) of 120 seconds, enforce single-use consumption rules, and are managed in-memory via ChallengeStore MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 75-79 Consent Tracking: Recorded via POST /consent and persisted in file-based JSON storage utilizing atomic file writes and intra-process locking mechanisms to prevent race conditions MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 78-79 Session Lifecycle: Managed through POST /session/start and POST /verify/session. Sessions have a sliding expiration (defaulting to 15 minutes) tracked in the SessionStore MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 119-120 Signals across requests are accumulated, and historical keystroke metrics are updated against the user's EMA profile MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 121-126 Sources: MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 72-126 3. Risk Scoring and Decision Outcomes The decision engine evaluates aggregated biometric deviation scores and contextual threat indicators through the SessionRiskEvaluator and supporting risk policies README.md 21 MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 121-124 Based on configurable risk weights, country-of-origin rules, and network threat flags, the evaluator outputs one of three explicit decisions: allow: The aggregate risk score falls below the primary threshold, and all mandatory biometric checks validate successfully. The session is authorized. step_up (or step-up): Moderate risk or partial biometric mismatch is detected. The session requires secondary verification (e.g., repeating a voice challenge or facial liveness check) before full access is granted MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 122-123 deny: High risk scores, blacklisted IP ranges, active Tor/proxy detection, or severe biometric verification failures trigger an immediate termination of the request or session. Sources: README.md 14 MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md 121-124 4. pages.searchText: Python Process Bridge Relevant source files apps/securekit-api/Services/CardOptions.cs apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs The Python Process Bridge is the subsystem responsible for managing the lifecycle, input/output streaming, and error handling of external Python biometric verification workers (CardPython, FacePython, VoicePython, KeystrokePython) from the ASP.NET Core backend. It handles process discovery across virtual environments, establishes JSON-lines-based communication over standard input/output, enforces strict execution timeouts, and guarantees process-tree termination to prevent zombie worker processes. 1. Worker Discovery and Environment Resolution The C# orchestration layer discovers and launches Python runtimes dynamically based on configuration parameters and local workspace conventions. The CardOptions class resolves paths for the script, temporary directories, and fallback search paths [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardOptions.cs:12-25]. The CardPython implementation iterates through a prioritized list of runtime candidate locations (Candidates()), evaluating virtual environments (.venv-card, .venv) before falling back to system-level interpreters (py -3, python3, python) [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:22-43]. If a dependency failure occurs (such as a missing Python package), the process bridge captures standard error output and translates the exception into a structured HTTP-mapped failure response [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:27-31, 80-87]. Sources: apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs 18-43 apps/securekit-api/Services/CardOptions.cs 12-25 2. CLI Contracts and Stdin/Stdout JSON-Lines Protocol Once a worker process is spawned, communication is established via a synchronous, line-oriented JSON protocol over standard input and standard output streams. As implemented in CardPython.Converse, the worker launches with the --worker flag and emits a stream of newline-delimited JSON objects [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:57-58, 99-128]. The protocol requires a two-phase handshake: Readiness Phase: The C# process reads stdout until it receives an event where event equals ready and ok is true [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:115-120]. Conversation Phase: Upon receiving readiness, the C# process writes the payload request object (assigned id: "1") to standard input (process.StandardInput) and awaits the matching response line on standard output [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:102-127]. Diyagramı büyütmek için seçin ↗ Sources: apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs 45-76 apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs 99-128 3. Timeouts, Error Handling, and Process-Tree Termination To prevent hanging worker threads or leaked OS resources during intensive computer vision tasks, CardPython wraps execution in linked cancellation tokens and process job containers. Timeouts: A CancellationTokenSource is bound to options.TimeoutMs (defaulting to 300,000ms / 5 minutes) [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:60-61]. If execution exceeds this window, an OperationCanceledException is intercepted and converted into a PYTHON_TIMEOUT failure code (504 Gateway Timeout) [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:77-78]. Process-Tree Kill: ProcessJob.Attach(process) registers the child process within a job object [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:68]. In the finally cleanup block, if the process has not exited, process.Kill(true) is invoked recursively to terminate the entire process tree, preventing orphaned Python sub-processes [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:88-96]. Stderr Drainage: Standard error is drained asynchronously via DrainError to prevent pipe deadlocks when stderr buffers fill up during exceptions or warnings [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:69]. Sources: [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardPython.cs:60-96] 4. Temporary Files and Data Flow Biometric verification pipelines often ingest high-resolution image or audio payloads. The process bridge coordinates data handoff by streaming inputs directly or referencing managed paths validated by CardOptions.Allowed [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardOptions.cs:28-41]. Path security constraints ensure that referenced reference images and temporary upload paths reside strictly within permitted roots (ReferenceDirectory, UserReferenceDirectory), preventing directory traversal vulnerabilities prior to spawning worker CLI arguments [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardOptions.cs:15-16, 24-41]. Sources: [apps/securekit-api/Services/CardOptions.cs:12-42]

pages.searchText: Storage and Configuration Relevant source files apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md Purpose and Scope This section covers the storage mechanisms and configuration infrastructure of the SecureKit ASP.NET Core API (apps/securekit-api). SecureKit utilizes lightweight file-based JSON stores (FileUserStore, ProfileStorage, and FixedKeystrokeStore) to manage user records, biometric profiles, and keystroke templates without requiring an external database. Configuration is managed via appsettings.json and extended through hierarchical environment variable overrides, enforcing security boundaries via strict reference root validation and atomic write guarantees. Sources: docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md:34-37, apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json:1-35 File-Based JSON Stores and Concurrency The storage subsystem relies on local file persistence to store state across restarts. By default, stores are initialized under the apps/securekit-api/.securekit directory or overridden via specific environment variables docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 34 Key components of the storage layer include: FileUserStore: Manages user credentials, salts, and identity hashes. The file path is configurable via SECUREKIT_USERS_FILE docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 43 ProfileStorage: Stores multi-modal biometric profile mappings, tracked via SECUREKIT_PROFILE_STORE docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 44 FixedKeystrokeStore: Manages fixed keystroke templates and reference inputs, tracked via SECUREKIT_KEYSTROKE_STORE docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 45 To prevent race conditions and partial writes during concurrent requests, the storage layer employs atomic write patterns and process-level file locking. Sources: docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md:34-49 Configuration Architecture (appsettings.json) The API behavior is driven by structured configuration sections defined in apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json. The configuration schema maps directly to strongly-typed options classes used throughout the service layer. The configuration layout contains the following primary blocks: Logging: Defines Microsoft ASP.NET and default log levels apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json 2-7 Face: Controls face verification constraints, upload limits, timeout thresholds, device selection (auto), and GPU enforcement apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json 9-15 Voice: Configures speaker verification parameters, minimum enrollment samples, Whisper model tiers, and ECAPA-VoxCeleb embeddings apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json 16-26 Card: Defines OCR timeouts, upload limits, and default matching thresholds apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json 27-31 Cors: Manages allowed cross-origin resource sharing policies apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json 32-34 Sources: apps/securekit-api/appsettings.json:1-35 Environment Variable Overrides and Reference Roots ASP.NET Core allows overriding any hierarchical configuration key using double-underscore (__) syntax in environment variables. This mechanism is heavily used for deployment customization, file path redirection, and strict boundary enforcement for biometric references. Important environment variables and path mappings include: SECUREKIT_USERS_FILE: Absolute path override for the user store docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 43 SECUREKIT_PROFILE_STORE: Absolute path override for user profiles docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 44 SECUREKIT_KEYSTROKE_STORE: Directory path for fixed keystroke models docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 45 Face__ReferenceDirectory / FACE_SLIDING_REFERENCES_ROOT: Storage roots for face embedding references docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 46-47 Card__UserReferenceDirectory: Storage root for verified ID card templates docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 48 Face__AllowedReferenceRoots__0 / Card__AllowedReferenceRoots__0: Explicit security constraints restricting file access to authorized reference directories docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 58-59 MOCK_IP_CHECK: Flag to bypass live IP/VPN geolocation checks during development docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 49 Sources: docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md:43-60

pages.title: @securekit/core Contracts and Orchestration
pages.searchText: @securekit/core Contracts and Orchestration Relevant source files README.md docs/NODE_API_CONTRACT_INVENTORY.md The @securekit/core package serves as the foundational shared TypeScript library within the SecureKit monorepo. It establishes the domain models, request/response contracts, biometric signal interfaces, risk evaluation policies, and orchestration logic utilized by both server-side implementations (packages/node-auth, apps/securekit-api) and client-side SDKs (packages/web-sdk). 1. Shared Request and Response Contracts The core package defines standard data transfer objects (DTOs) and state interfaces for user lifecycle management, challenge issuance, consent verification, and multi-modal profile storage. Key structural definitions encompass: User Records & Profiles: Standardized schemas for userId, registration timestamps, consent versions, and profile associations (keystroke models, face embeddings, voice references, and card metadata). Identifiers are consistently normalized (trimmed and lowercased where appropriate) across authentication boundaries. Challenges: Structures governing challenge generation, including language parameters (lang), string lengths (length), dynamic word counts (wordCount), and strict time-to-live (CHALLENGE_TTL_SECONDS) constraints. Session Lifecycle: Time-bound session handles (sessionId) tracking expiration windows (SESSION_TTL_SECONDS), accumulated signal states, and evaluation outcomes. Figure 1: Contract Validation and Orchestration Flow Sources: README.md:19-21, docs/NODE_API_CONTRACT_INVENTORY.md:30-52 2. Biometrics Modules and Signal Models Biometric and contextual data are encapsulated into structured signal payloads before being passed to verification services or risk evaluators. The core contracts define uniform schemas for: Keystroke Dynamics: Timings for keydown and keyup events, measuring hold durations and transition latencies to match against Exponential Moving Average (EMA) user profiles or fixed-text templates. Facial and Voice Signals: Embeddings, reference image paths, liveness indicators, and speech-to-text verification payloads evaluated by external Python subprocesses. Network and Location Signals: IP metadata structures containing flags for VPN, proxy, Tor, or relay usage, alongside geographic drift calculations and country-code allowances (allowedCountries). Signal Processing and Module Mapping to Code Entities Sources: README.md:9-14, docs/NODE_API_CONTRACT_INVENTORY.md:69-76 3. Risk Policies and Default Configuration (defaultPolicy) The risk policy engine calculates session trust scores and determines whether an authentication attempt is permitted, denied, or requires step-up verification. The defaultPolicy configuration dictates threshold rules and security constraints: Risk Score Bounds: Defines numeric boundaries such as allowMaxRisk and denyMinRisk to categorize aggregated signal scores. Network Enforcement: Parameters like treatVpnAsFailure and minNetworkScore dictate strict denial or penalization when non-residential or proxy IP flags are raised. Step-Up Requirements: Specifies stepUpSteps array mappings, identifying secondary verification modalities (e.g., voice challenge, face re-verification) required when risk scores fall into intermediate bands. Decision Outcomes: Yields discrete resolution values: allow, step_up, or deny for dynamic evaluations, and accept or reject for fixed-text verifications. Sources: docs/NODE_API_CONTRACT_INVENTORY.md:27-29, docs/NODE_API_CONTRACT_INVENTORY.md:69-76 4. The Orchestration Engine The orchestrator coordinates state persistence, incremental signal aggregation, and policy enforcement across an active authentication session. When a verification request is submitted, the orchestrator executes the following sequence: Retrieves the active session state from the underlying storage layer (SessionStore). Appends or merges incoming telemetry signals (signalsUsed) with historical session data. Invokes the risk evaluation service (SessionRiskEvaluator) against the active policy profile (defaultPolicy). Generates a unified decision (decision), computes the resulting riskScore, and compiles any required step-up actions (requiredSteps) or diagnostic reasons (reasons). pages.searchText: Face and Voice Workers Relevant source files MIGRATION_TO_ASPNET10_PLAN.md README.md This page details the implementation of the face and voice biometric workers within the SecureKit toolkit. These Python-based workers handle the core logic for face enrollment/verification using MTCNN and FaceNet, and voice enrollment/verification using Whisper and SpeechBrain. They are invoked by the ASP.NET Core API via a controlled process bridge. Face Verification Worker The face verification worker, located at python/face_verification/face_verification.py python/face_verification/face_verification.py 1-177 is responsible for detecting faces, extracting face embeddings, and comparing them for verification. It utilizes the MTCNN (Multi-task Cascaded Convolutional Networks) for face detection and FaceNet for generating high-dimensional face embeddings. Implementation Details The face_verification.py script can operate in two main modes: Enrollment: Takes an image, detects a face, and returns its embedding. Verification: Takes a reference embedding and a probe image, detects a face in the probe, extracts its embedding, and calculates the similarity between the two embeddings. The script uses argparse python/face_verification/face_verification.py 130-147 to handle command-line arguments for specifying the operation mode (--enroll or --verify), input files (--image, --reference, --probe), and output format (--json). Key components and their roles: FaceDetector class: python/face_verification/face_verification.py 16-40 Initializes the MTCNN model for face detection. The detect_face method python/face_verification/face_verification.py 29-40 takes an image (as a NumPy array) and returns the bounding box coordinates of the detected face. FaceEmbedder class: python/face_verification/face_verification.py 43-67 Initializes the FaceNet model for embedding generation. The get_embedding method python/face_verification/face_verification.py 56-67 takes a cropped face image and returns its 512-dimensional embedding. FaceVerifier class: python/face_verification/face_verification.py 70-100 Orchestrates the face detection and embedding process. The enroll method python/face_verification/face_verification.py 79-84 detects a face in an image and returns its embedding. The verify method python/face_verification/face_verification.py 86-100 takes a reference embedding and a probe image, extracts the probe's embedding, and calculates the cosine similarity between them. It also applies a configurable threshold (FACE_VERIFICATION_THRESHOLD) to determine if the faces match. The script also includes basic liveness detection by checking for a single, well-defined face in the image. If multiple faces are detected or no face is found, it returns an error. Data Flow The ASP.NET Core API invokes the face_verification.py script as a child process. It uses Whisper for speech-to-text transcription to ensure the spoken phrase matches a challenge text, and SpeechBrain for speaker verification to compare voice characteristics. Implementation Details The voice_verification.py script supports two primary operations: Enrollment: Takes an audio file and a challenge text, transcribes the audio using Whisper, verifies it against the challenge, and then extracts a speaker embedding using SpeechBrain. Verification: Takes an audio file, a challenge text, and a reference speaker embedding. It transcribes the audio, verifies it against the challenge, extracts a speaker embedding from the audio, and compares it to the reference embedding. The script uses argparse python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 160-177 for command-line argument parsing, allowing specification of operation mode (--enroll or --verify), input audio (--audio), challenge text (--challenge), and reference embedding (--reference). Key components and their roles: SpeechToText class: python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 16-40 Initializes the Whisper model for speech transcription. The transcribe method python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 29-40 takes an audio file path and returns the transcribed text. SpeakerEmbedder class: python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 43-67 Initializes the SpeechBrain speaker verification model. The get_embedding method python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 56-67 takes an audio file path and returns a speaker embedding. VoiceVerifier class: python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 70-109 Orchestrates the transcription and speaker embedding processes. The enroll method python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 82-92 transcribes audio, checks against the challenge, and extracts a speaker embedding. The verify method python/voice_verification/voice_verification.py 94-109 performs transcription, challenge verification, extracts a probe embedding, and calculates cosine similarity with a reference embedding. It uses VOICE_VERIFICATION_THRESHOLD for similarity comparison. The script ensures that the transcribed text matches the provided challenge text, adding a layer of liveness and intent verification. Data Flow Similar to the face worker, the ASP.NET Core API communicates with the voice_verification.py script via a process bridge. pages.searchText: IP Check and Environment Setup Relevant source files scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs scripts/biometric-preflight.py Purpose and Scope This page details the environment setup, dependency management, virtual environments (.venv-face, .venv-voice, .venv-card), GPU/CUDA configuration, FFmpeg integration, and network/IP check infrastructure (including VPNAPI signals and ip_check.py) for SecureKit's Python biometric and intelligence workers. It explains how system preflight checks validate these dependencies before runtime execution. 1. Python Virtual Environments and Dependency Isolation SecureKit segregates Python dependencies into dedicated virtual environments per biometric modality (.venv-face, .venv-voice, .venv-card). This isolation prevents library version conflicts and Windows DLL collision issues—such as those occurring when PyTorch is imported alongside PaddleOCR. The preflight module validator defines explicit dependency requirements for each modality: Face: numpy, PIL, torch, torchvision, facenet_pytorch scripts/biometric-preflight.py 8-9 Voice: numpy, torch, torchaudio, whisper, speechbrain, imageio_ffmpeg scripts/biometric-preflight.py 10 Card: numpy, PIL, cv2, yaml, rapidfuzz, skimage, torch, open_clip, paddle, paddleocr scripts/biometric-preflight.py 13 Sources: scripts/biometric-preflight.py 8-14 2. Preflight Probing Architecture The preflight runner scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs orchestrates environment probing by spawning isolated Python subprocesses executing scripts/biometric-preflight.py scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs 12-37 Probing Data Flow Node Launcher: biometric-preflight.mjs checks environment variables (*_PYTHON_BIN), local .venv-* paths, and system python3 or py launchers scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs 40-48 Subprocess Spawn: Spawns python scripts/biometric-preflight.py <module> with isolated stdio and safety timeouts (45 seconds) scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs 12-20 Import Safety: biometric-preflight.py captures stdout/stderr during importlib.import_module() calls to prevent leaking local configuration paths or throwing unhandled import side-effects scripts/biometric-preflight.py 21-25 Report Generation: Results are parsed from JSON output and written to .run-logs/biometric-preflight.json scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs 30-58 Sources: scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs 12-37 scripts/biometric-preflight.py 15-26 3. Hardware Requirements: GPU/CUDA and FFmpeg GPU and CUDA Validation For face and voice modalities, biometric-preflight.py inspects PyTorch CUDA availability (torch.cuda.is_available()) scripts/biometric-preflight.py 27-33 Configuration parameters like FACE_DEVICE, FACE_REQUIRE_GPU, or Face__RequireGpu dictate whether GPU acceleration is strictly required scripts/biometric-preflight.py 30-31 If REQUIRE_GPU is enabled, preflight checks fail if CUDA is absent. FFmpeg Requirements Voice verification relies heavily on audio preprocessing via FFmpeg. The preflight check verifies FFmpeg availability using shutil.which("ffmpeg"), with an automatic fallback to binaries bundled by imageio_ffmpeg scripts/biometric-preflight.py 34-44 Sources: scripts/biometric-preflight.py 27-44 4. IP Check and VPNAPI Signals Network verification and IP intelligence modules (ip_check.py) evaluate client connection metadata to assess fraud risk during authentication sessions. Key Signal Categories VPN / Proxy Detection: Queries IP intelligence providers (such as VPNAPI) to flag commercial VPN exits, data centers, and anonymous proxy ranges. Geolocation Risk: Validates client IP geographic origin against expected user profiles or session bounds. Threat Scoring: Computes aggregate risk scores incorporated into SessionRiskEvaluator. pages.title: Biometric Preflight
pages.searchText: Biometric Preflight Relevant source files scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs scripts/biometric-preflight.py Overview and Scope The Biometric Preflight subsystem (scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs and scripts/biometric-preflight.py) provides automated validation of runtime environments, third-party python dependencies, hardware acceleration (CUDA), and external system binaries (such as ffmpeg) required by SecureKit's multimodal biometric verification workers. Before spinning up Python subprocess bridges in the ASP.NET Core API or legacy Node backend, the preflight script executes a series of safe, non-invasive probes that verify module importability without loading heavy ML weights into memory or downloading model checkpoints. pages.searchText: .NET Test Suite Relevant source files apps/securekit-api.tests/HealthTests.cs apps/securekit-api.tests/StageSevenTests.cs The .NET Test Suite (apps/securekit-api.tests) is the integration and unit testing framework for the SecureKit ASP.NET Core API (apps/securekit-api). It validates controller endpoints, service layers, biometric Python process bridges, error translation contracts, and health monitors against expected behaviors and legacy Node.js API parity. Test Architecture and Support Infrastructure The test suite relies heavily on Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing to spin up in-memory instances of the API using WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint>. Custom test fixtures and helpers like ContractAssert validate JSON response shapes, HTTP status codes, and error structures. For stage-specific tests, such as card verification integration (StageSevenTests), tests instantiate specialized web application factories that isolate file system operations, mock Python script execution paths, and override configuration keys (such as SECUREKIT_PROFILE_STORE, Card:ReferenceDirectory, and Card:ScriptPath). pages.searchText: Glossary Relevant source files README.md docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md docs/BIOMETRIC_ACCEPTANCE.md Purpose and Scope This page defines core terminology specific to the SecureKit multi-modal biometric authentication toolkit. It details the technical implementation, data flows, configuration parameters, and architectural patterns behind each concept, linking them directly to code entities across the monorepo. Sources: README.md 1-145 docs/BIOMETRIC_ACCEPTANCE.md 1-139 docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 1-110 1. Parity Stage and Parity Harness Parity stages (stage-one through stage-seven) represent incremental milestones used during the migration and contractual verification between the legacy Node/Express API (packages/node-auth) and the default ASP.NET Core 10 API (apps/securekit-api). The parity harness (aspnet-parity.mjs and related scripts) executes sequential HTTP contract comparisons against both backend implementations using automated fixtures. Data Flow: The test runner issues identical HTTP payloads across both backend endpoints, recording response structures, status codes, and headers into .run-logs/aspnet-parity.json. Key Functions/Classes: Parity validation runner scripts located in packages/node-auth/scripts/ and C# integration test suites under apps/securekit-api.tests. Diyagramı büyütmek için seçin ↗ Sources: docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 76-102 2. Biometric Manifest A manifest is a JSON configuration structure (manifest.json) utilized by the biometric acceptance testing framework to declare paths, sample metadata, and verification parameters for face, voice, and card evaluation pipelines without exposing raw personally identifiable information (PII) or embedding vectors to the Git repository. Implementation: Managed via preparation scripts (scripts/biometric-acceptance-prepare.mjs) and validated by the acceptance engine (scripts/biometric-acceptance.mjs). Data Flow: The manifest specifies file locations under .run-logs/acceptance/samples. The runner loads these samples, initializes an isolated temporary C# API instance, and validates HTTP contract responses against predefined success criteria. Diyagramı büyütmek için seçin ↗ Sources: docs/BIOMETRIC_ACCEPTANCE.md 56-128 3. Biometric Preflight Preflight refers to the environment verification phase executed prior to real biometric acceptance tests (scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs and .py). It checks runtime dependencies, CUDA availability, binary path resolutions, and FFmpeg integration. Implementation: Performs non-destructive dependency checking (e.g., verifying Python imports for FaceNet, Whisper, SpeechBrain, and PaddleOCR) without downloading model weights or parsing raw user images. Key Files: scripts/biometric-preflight.mjs, producing output logs at .run-logs/biometric-preflight.json. Sources: docs/BIOMETRIC_ACCEPTANCE.md 8-39 4. Model and Hardware Acceptance Model and hardware acceptance designates the phase of verification where actual deep-learning models (MTCNN, FaceNet, Whisper, SpeechBrain, OpenCLIP, PaddleOCR) and host hardware accelerators (CPU, CUDA GPUs) execute real inference pipelines. Distinction: Unlike protocol fixture tests (apps/securekit-api.tests), which validate JSON serialization and routing contracts, model acceptance evaluates numerical embedding similarity, liveness detection, optical character recognition accuracy, and hardware throughput under constraints defined by FACE_DEVICE, VOICE_DEVICE, and timeout configurations. Sources: docs/BIOMETRIC_ACCEPTANCE.md NaN-NaN 5. Challenge TTL and Challenge Store Challenge TTL (Time-To-Live) and the Challenge Store manage time-sensitive, single-use authentication challenges (such as speech verification challenge phrases or cryptographic nonces). Implementation: Challenges are generated server-side, assigned an expiration timestamp (TTL), stored in an in-memory or session-backed repository (ChallengeStore), and invalidated immediately upon verification attempt or timeout. Sources: README.md NaN-NaN 6. Step-Up Authentication (step_up) step_up is an intermediary authentication decision outcome generated by the risk evaluation engine when baseline multi-factor signals are insufficient, ambiguous, or indicate elevated risk. Decision Model: The risk engine evaluates aggregated signals (keystroke dynamics, face match score, IP/network reputation) to produce one of three outcomes: allow, step_up, or deny. A step_up result forces the client SDK to prompt for an additional biometric modality (e.g., voice or card verification) before session promotion. Diyagramı büyütmek için seçin ↗ Sources: README.md 13-14 7. Sliding Window Face Reference Management Sliding window face refers to a reference management strategy for face biometric profiles where historical embedding vectors are dynamically updated or rotated using a rolling window mechanism (FACE_SLIDING_REFERENCES_ROOT). Implementation: Rather than relying strictly on a single static enrollment image, the sliding window approach maintains a bounded set of reference embeddings, accommodating gradual changes in appearance, lighting, or angles over time while bounding storage growth. Sources: docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 46-47 8. Exponential Moving Average (EMA) Keystroke Profile An EMA keystroke profile utilizes an Exponential Moving Average algorithm to continuously adapt and update a user's typing rhythm baseline (keydown / keyup hold and flight times) across authentication sessions. Data Flow: Each successful authentication updates the user's keystroke feature vector by blending historical profile weights with the incoming sample measurements via exponential weighting, allowing the system to adapt to natural variations in typing behavior over time. Sources: README.md 9-10 9. Reference Roots Reference roots (Face__AllowedReferenceRoots__0, Card__AllowedReferenceRoots__0) are explicit filesystem directory whitelists configured in ASP.NET Core (appsettings.json or environment variables) that restrict where the API can read or write biometric reference images and OCR templates. Security Role: Enforces strict filesystem sandboxing, ensuring that biometric storage paths cannot be manipulated via path-traversal attacks through request payloads. Sources: docs/ASPNET_CUTOVER.md 57-59 10. Worker Bridge The worker bridge is the inter-process communication layer where C# verification services invoke isolated Python worker processes (CardPython, FacePython, VoicePython, KeystrokePython) via standard input/output (stdin/stdout) CLI contracts and temporary file exchanges. Data Flow: C# services serialize input payloads or pass temporary file paths to specialized Python worker scripts, enforce strict execution timeouts (VOICE_PYTHON_TIMEOUT_MS, CARD_PYTHON_TIMEOUT_MS), manage process-tree termination, and parse structured JSON responses returned via stdout.
